title: "We've Always Done It This Way"
objective: After this level you can spot the appeal to tradition and explain when a long track record is, and isn't, a good reason.
summary: Bloodletting lasted from antiquity to the 1800s without working as claimed. The appeal to tradition treats 'we've always done it' as proof; Chesterton's fence says find the reason first.

cards.headline: From ancient times until the 1800s, doctors drained blood from the sick.
cards.body: Bloodletting was meant to balance the body's "humors", fluids once thought to govern health. Generation after generation of doctors used it. Surely a treatment trusted for that long must work?

cards.headline: What the track record hid
cards.body: Being used for centuries is not the same as being tested. When the physician Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis studied the results, publishing first in 1828, he found bloodletting was not as effective as its supporters claimed. Even then, tradition let go slowly: some medical textbooks still recommended it as late as 1942.

cards.headline: The appeal to tradition
cards.body: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls it the fallacy of traditional wisdom: saying a practice must be fine today simply because it was the apparently wise practice in the past. Note the careful word simply. The encyclopedia grants that a tradition is some reason, just not always a good enough one, for instance when conditions have changed. "We've always done it this way" can start a conversation. It can't end one.

cards.headline: Chesterton's fence
cards.body: So when does a track record count? In his 1929 book The Thing, G. K. Chesterton imagined a fence across a road. A reformer who says "I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away" should first go and find out its use. A tradition may hold a reason nobody remembers. Find the reason, then judge it on its merits, as Louis did with bloodletting.

cards.headline: Appeal to tradition: spotted
learned: Bloodletting lasted centuries without working as claimed
Tradition alone doesn't make a practice right
A tradition is some reason, not always enough
Chesterton: find the reason before you remove it

questions.prompt: What does the fallacy of traditional wisdom assume?

options.label: Every new idea is better than an old one
A practice is fine now just because it's old
Traditions carry no information at all
options.rationale: The IEP says tradition is some reason.

options.label: Experts must approve every old custom
options.rationale: Experts don't come into this fallacy.

questions.explanation: It says a practice must be OK today simply because it was the apparently wise practice in the past.

questions.prompt: Put these in order, from earliest to latest, in the bloodletting story.
questions.explanation: Louis studied bloodletting's results, publishing first in 1828. Chesterton imagined his fence in 1929, and some medical textbooks still recommended bloodletting as late as 1942.

questions.prompt: By Chesterton's fence, what should you do before scrapping an old school rule nobody can explain?

options.label: Scrap it at once, since nobody can explain it
options.rationale: That's the reformer Chesterton warns about.

options.label: Keep it forever, since it's old
Find out why it was made, then judge that reason
Ask which students like it most

questions.explanation: Chesterton: find the fence's use before clearing it away. The tradition is a question to answer, not a proof.
